blocks.text: Also called BFS on trees visit every node level by level, left to right, using a queue.

Level Order Traversal visits nodes of a binary tree level by level starting from the root (level 0), then all nodes at level 1, then level 2, and so on. Within each level, nodes are visited left to right.
It is essentially Breadth-First Search (BFS) applied to a tree. The key data structure that makes this work is a Queue (FIFO First In First Out).
DFS goes deep first (down a branch). BFS goes wide first (across a level). Level order = BFS = queue. This one sentence is worth memorising.

items: Level 0: BFS starts from the root node1. Since this is the first level, the result becomes [1].
Level 1: After visiting the root, BFS visits all of its children from left to right. The nodes at this level are 2 and 3, so the result becomes [1, 2, 3].
Level 2: Next, BFS visits all children of nodes2and3. These nodes are 4, 5, 6, and 7, so the result becomes [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
Level-by-Level Processing: BFS always completes one level before moving to the next. It never goes deep into a branch until all nodes at the current level have been visited.
Final Level Order Traversal: The nodes are visited in the order 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7.

blocks.text: Why a Queue is Used: A queue follows the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle. Nodes are added to the back of the queue and processed from the front, ensuring they are visited level by level.
The queue is the engine of level order traversal. Here's exactly what happens at each step.
The rule is simple: dequeue a node, process it, then enqueue its left and right children (if they exist).
Step 1: Enqueue root
We start by adding the root node (1) to the queue. Since BFS always begins from the root, it is the first node waiting to be processed.
Step 2: Dequeue 1, enqueue its children 2 and 3
Remove1from the front of the queue and add it to the output. Then enqueue its children (2and3) so they can be processed later.
At this point, Level 0 has been completely processed.
Step 3: Dequeue 2, enqueue children 4 and 5
Remove2from the queue and add it to the output. Then enqueue its children (4and5) to the back of the queue
Notice that3stays ahead of4and5because it was added earlier.
Step 4: Dequeue 3, enqueue children 6 and 7
Remove3from the queue and add it to the output. Then enqueue its children (6and7).
Now all nodes at Level 1 have been processed.
Steps 5-8: Dequeue 4, 5, 6, 7 (all leaves, no children to enqueue)
Remove4,5,6, and7one by one and add them to the output. Since they are leaf nodes, no new nodes are added to the queue.

Code Implementation
The template is always the same: use a queue, process node by node, push children.
Output:
Most interview problems ask for output grouped by level a list of lists. The trick is to check the queue size before the inner loop, which tells you exactly how many nodes are in the current level.

Time Complexity

Time Complexity: O(n): Every node is visited exactly once during the traversal. Each node is added to the queue once and removed from the queue once, so the total work is proportional to the number of nodes in the tree.
Space Complexity
Space Complexity: O(w): The queue stores nodes level by level. At any moment, the maximum number of nodes in the queue equals the maximum width (w) of the tree.
In the worst case, such as a perfect binary tree, the last level contains about half of all nodes. Therefore, the queue may hold O(n) nodes, making the worst-case space complexity O(n).
Once you know the template, the following problem types are just variations of it.

blocks.text: Right Side View: The right side view contains the last node visible at each level when looking at the tree from the right. During BFS, simply save the last node processed at every level.
Zigzag Traversal: Zigzag traversal visits levels in alternating directions. One level is read left-to-right, the next right-to-left, and this pattern continues for all levels.
Level Averages: Level averages find the average value of nodes at each level. For every level, add all node values together and divide by the number of nodes in that level.
Minimum Depth: The minimum depth is the shortest distance from the root to a leaf node. In BFS, the first leaf node encountered automatically gives the minimum depth.
Maximum Width: The maximum width is the largest number of positions occupied by nodes at any level. It is calculated by tracking the first and last node positions in each level.
Null Sentinel: A null sentinel is a special marker added to the queue to indicate the end of a level. While it works, using thelevel_sizeapproach is simpler and more commonly preferred in interviews

items: Forgetting to check if (!root) return causes crash on empty tree.
Using a stack instead of a queue that gives DFS, not BFS.
Not capturing level_size before the inner loop queue grows mid-loop and you process too many nodes per level.
Pushing null children into the queue always guard with if (node.left).
Forgetting that the result is 0-indexed for levels but problems sometimes say "level 1 = root".
